<p>As of Sept. 14, 2026, the <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/newsroom/department-of-health-provides-statewide-update-091126">Pennsylvania Department of Health</a> has confirmed 693 measles cases across 38 of the state’s 67 counties this year, including 133 hospitalizations and four deaths <a href="https://www.statnews.com/2026/09/15/fourth-measles-death-pennsylvania-acute-disseminated-encephalomyelitis">among unvaccinated residents</a>. That compares with 16 cases statewide in all of 2025.</p>

<p>Allegheny County reported its first case tied to the current outbreak in August, when the county health department <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/News-Articles/Allegheny-County-Press-Releases/August-2026-PR/08-20-2026-Potential-Measles-Exposure-Statement">warned of a potential exposure</a> at UPMC Children’s Hospital’s emergency department. Two confirmed cases were diagnosed on Aug. 27, 2026, but the patients left the county afterward.</p>

<p>Pittsburgh is where <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-world-risks-forgetting-one-of-humanitys-greatest-triumphs-as-polio-nears-global-eradication-70-years-after-jonas-salk-developed-the-vaccine-in-a-pittsburgh-lab-270042">Dr. Jonas Salk developed the first polio vaccine</a> on the campus of the University of Pittsburgh. <a href="https://www.post-gazette.com/opinion/insight/2023/03/26/pittsburgh-polio-prepioneers-salk-vaccine/stories/202303260025">Children throughout the Pittsburgh area</a>, including my father, lined up to participate in the <a href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/april-26/polio-vaccine-trials-begin">Salk vaccine trials</a> in 1954.  </p>

<p>That history offers a useful lens for understanding today’s measles outbreak: what’s driving it, how it spreads, and what residents in the Pittsburgh area need to know.</p>

<h2>Measles, explained</h2>

<p>Measles is one of the oldest and most contagious diseases. In fact, measles was around when the <a href="https://scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&amp;pid=S0256-95742010000400013">Egyptian pyramids were being built</a>. Archaeological evidence shows the measles virus <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aba9411">in the Tigris and Euphrates river valley in 3000 B.C.E</a>. </p>

<p>Measles is an acute respiratory virus. If an unvaccinated individual who has never had measles is exposed to the measles virus, they will likely become sick. Measles easily spreads through the air. Infected individuals are contagious 3-5 days before symptoms occur, a transmission mechanism known as asymptomatic spread. Viral particles remain <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/causes/index.html">active and infectious for up to two hours</a> after a person with measles leaves a room.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A small vial is held between a person's thumb and forefinger." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759737/original/file-20260914-50-85sfqe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The measles was eliminated from the U.S. in 2000 through the effective use of the vaccine.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/vial-of-the-measles-mumps-and-rubella-vaccination-for-news-photo/2242752228?adppopup=true">PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Symptoms of measles include a fever as high as 105 degrees Fahrenheit, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/ency/imagepages/2558.htm#:%7E:text=Koplik%20spots%20are%20seen%20with,in%20the%20course%20of%20measles.">Koplik spots</a>, which are small white or bluish-white spots that appear on the inside of the cheeks before the measles rash breaks out on the skin. These spots are the <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK549793/">defining diagnostic feature of measles</a>. Measles also results in a rash, known as a “bucket of paint rash” because it looks like someone spilled a bucket of red paint over the head of the sick person. </p>

<p>The rash is not contagious. This disease spreads when someone breathes in the virus.</p>

<p>Before there was a vaccine for measles, upward of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html">3 million people – mostly children – were infected in the U.S. each year, 48,000 were hospitalized, and as many as 500 died</a>. </p>

<p>Measles was <a href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/measles-elimination-status-what-it-is-and-how-the-u-s-could-lose-it/">eliminated in the United States through vaccination in 2000</a>, meaning person-to-person spread of the disease was disrupted. However, due to <a href="https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/health/documents/topics/documents/programs/immunizations/School%20Immunization%20Survey%20Summary%20for%20PA%202025-2026.pdf">declining vaccination rates</a>, measles is once again spreading throughout Pennsylvania, resulting in approximately <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">four times as many measles cases in 2026</a> within the state as in the previous 30 years combined. </p>

<p>Measles vaccination rates <a href="https://www.haponline.org/News/HAP-News-Articles/Latest-News/school-age-vaccination-rates-decline-in-pa-nation">need to be above 95%</a> to prevent the disease from spreading. The current outbreak has affected a <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">majority of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties</a>, an indicator that even small declines in vaccination coverage result in large outbreaks.</p>

<p>The MMR vaccine is covered at no cost by most private insurance plans and is available free of charge to Medicaid-insured, uninsured or underinsured children at any of <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/about-us/state-health-centers#sortCriteria=%40copapwptitle%20ascending%2C%40title%20ascending%2C%40copapwpeducatorname%20ascending">Pennsylvania’s 59 state health centers</a>. The <a href="https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/measles/measles-vaccine/">American Academy of Pediatrics recommends</a> children receive two doses by ages 4 to 6 to ensure protection against measles.  </p>

<p>Allegheny County’s <a href="https://www.wesanews.org/health-science-tech/2025-09-30/routine-vaccination-rates-decline-pennsylvania-kindergarteners">kindergarten MMR vaccination rate</a> was <a href="https://www.alleghenycounty.us/files/assets/county/v/4/government/health/documents/vaccine-coverage/2025-to-2026-immunization-report.pdf">91.8% for the 2025-26 school year</a> – <a href="https://theconversation.com/cdc-vs-pennsylvania-why-conflicting-public-health-messages-jeopardize-public-safety-291239">below the 95% threshold</a> needed to stop measles from spreading and part of a decline the county health department has tracked for <a href="https://cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/allegheny-county-vaccination-rate-slipping">more than a decade</a>. </p>

<h2>If you’re exposed to measles</h2>

<p>If you are vaccinated or have had measles, there is little risk – <a href="https://www.nfid.org/resource/frequently-asked-questions-about-measles/">about 3%</a> – that you will develop measles if exposed to the virus. There is no need to quarantine, but even vaccinated people should watch for symptoms of disease. </p>

<p>For people who are unvaccinated, including infants, the risk of developing a measles infection after exposure is <a href="https://www.nfid.org/resource/frequently-asked-questions-about-measles/">approximately 90%</a>. Unvaccinated individuals need to quarantine. Local health departments require them to stay away from others for 21 days to prevent the asymptomatic spread of disease.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A young boy receives a shot in the arm." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759739/original/file-20260914-50-l5kr4j.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">About 15% of Pennsylvania children who got the measles this year had to be hospitalized.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/xerius-jackson-age-7-gets-an-mmr-vaccine-at-a-vaccine-news-photo/2202122494?adppopup=true">Getty Images News via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>If an individual in quarantine becomes ill, they will begin a minimum 14-day isolation. </p>

<p>Measles is a serious disease. Approximately 20% of people who get it will develop pneumonia; many will require hospitalization, and a few will die. Each measles case costs our healthcare system <a href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/2025/estimating-the-financial-costs-of-measles-outbreaks#">approximately US$43,000</a>, according to a Johns Hopkins systematic review of outbreaks in 18 states.</p>

<p>The measles virus also has the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aay6485">ability to suppress one’s immune system</a>. This means that after a bout of measles, survivors can be left more vulnerable to other infections they were previously protected against, sometimes for months or even years afterward.</p>

<p>In order to <a href="https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/measles/measles-vaccine/?srsltid=AfmBOor3jwP65Sbj2DSOyaYNrEc1unDgYFZF2aAY4dRGuSRrkc1bMZb0">prevent measles from spreading in our communities</a>, at <a href="https://www.kff.org/other-health/measles-elimination-status-what-it-is-and-how-the-u-s-could-lose-it/">least 95%</a> of the population must be vaccinated. The MMR vaccine was designed to prevent an individual from developing measles. But there is an added bonus: When the majority of a population is vaccinated, there are community-wide effects, mainly that <a href="https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles">community transmission of measles</a> will begin to decline.</p>

<p>Pittsburgh helped end one vaccine-preventable epidemic 70 years ago. The current measles outbreak could be a test of whether the local history still means something for vaccination rates today.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291098/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Middle East is the latest arena of political recalibration for Italy’s right-wing but pragmatic Meloni</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759741/original/file-20260914-50-fgapz3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C1024%2C682&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni after a meeting with Lebanon&#39;s Parliament speaker.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Lebanon%20Italy/1006d5a1eee74f5796cd5e47a6863132/photo">AP Photo/Bilal Hussein</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has made a political art of being many things at once.</p>

<p>Since coming to power in 2022, she has <a href="https://www.iai.it/en/publications/c05/meloni-between-trump-and-europe-limits-political-adaptability">become the leader</a> of Italy’s longest-serving postwar government. Meloni has also transformed herself from a politician once viewed as a radical outsider into one of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/sep/19/shapeshifter-who-is-the-real-giorgia-meloni-italy-prime-minister">Europe’s most consequential conservative leaders</a>. Her political strength has always rested on adaptability: whether speaking the culture war language of MAGA politics in Washington, European pragmatism in Brussels or nationalism in Rome.</p>

<p>Nowhere is that adaptability more visible than in her dealings in the Middle East.</p>

<p>Her government has long cultivated close relations with Israel and presented itself as <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/sep/19/shapeshifter-who-is-the-real-giorgia-meloni-italy-prime-minister">one of Israel’s strongest political supporters in Europe</a>. This position was in part self-serving for Meloni: As a leader of a party with <a href="https://theconversation.com/giorgia-meloni-the-political-provocateur-set-to-become-italys-first-far-right-leader-since-mussolini-190116">roots in Italy’s post-fascist right</a>, the approach to Israel – alongside repeated condemnations of anti-Semitism and the <a href="https://www.wantedinrome.com/news/italy-holocaust-remembrance-day-meloni-fascist-complicity-dark-page-italian-history.html">racial laws of the fascist regime</a> – signaled a break with the past. </p>

<p>Yet her strong support for Israel was increasingly at odds with public opinion at home, which <a href="https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2025/09/24/italy-doesnt-want-to-recognise-palestine-but-do-italians">moved sharply against Israel</a> as the war in Gaza ground on. Some 75% of Italians hold an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 66% in 2025, according to <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/06/04/most-people-across-36-countries-have-negative-views-of-israel-and-little-confidence-in-netanyahu/">a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey</a>. </p>

<p>Perhaps recognizing the yearslong shift, Meloni subtly changed course. In April 2026, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/italy-suspends-defence-cooperation-deal-with-israel-2026-04-14/">Italy suspended the automatic renewal</a> of its defense cooperation agreement with Israel. That followed growing public criticism of Israeli military actions in Gaza and Lebanon, including <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/italy-opposed-israeli-ground-operation-rafah-2024-03-19">an incident</a> in which Israeli forces fired warning shots at a clearly marked Italian U.N. convoy in southern Lebanon, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/italy-summons-israeli-ambassador-after-shots-fired-un-lebanon-2026-04-08/">damaging one vehicle but causing no injuries</a>.</p>

<p>It was the <a href="https://revdem.ceu.edu/2025/06/18/figaro-qui-figaro-qua/">kind of symbolic recalibration</a> that Meloni has increasingly used to position Italy as a geopolitical hinge between competing power centers in order to maximize Rome’s room for maneuver on the world stage. The Middle East has just given that strategy a new environment. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

<h2>From Jerusalem to Beirut</h2>

<p>None of that is to suggest that Meloni has in any way become an anti-Israel leader.</p>

<p>Diplomatically symbolic as it might have been, suspending the renewal of the defense cooperation agreement had almost no practical effect on Israel. Notwithstanding that and other occasional disagreements <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c998evlgz8ko">over things such Israeli settlement activity</a>, the two countries maintain close diplomatic and economic relations. </p>

<p>Italy, moreover, has been a <a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/interviste/2023/11/il-ministro-tajani-sosteniamo-la-difesa-di-israele-ma-bisogna-proteggere-i-civili-corriere-della-sera/">reliable backer</a> of Israel in international forums in the course of the war in Gaza. And notably, <a href="https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/foreign-secretary-oral-statement-on-israel-palestine?utm">Italy declined to join the U.K. and France</a> in banning goods from the occupied West Bank – an issue that has driven a wedge between EU members and Israel – though Italian Foreign Minister Antonio <a href="https://www.ansa.it/english/newswire/english_service/2026/04/23/italy-in-favour-of-restrictions-in-imports-from-west-bank-settlers-2_e06edbf6-80e4-414a-8e4d-eae2a77efd1f.html?utm">Tajani has said Rome is considering such measures</a>.</p>

<p>Instead, Meloni’s rhetoric on Israel appears to represent primarily a form of political and reputational management rather than a substantive policy shift. Yet it shows how Meloni is particularly receptive to political realities and looking for ways to make the case for Italy as a useful diplomatic partner that talks to all sides.</p>

<p>And here, Lebanon offers another clear example of her approach. </p>

<p>In August 2026, Meloni hosted Lebanese President Joseph Aoun <a href="https://qna.org.qa/en/news/news-details?id=italian-prime-minister-lebanese-president-discuss-situation-in-lebanon&amp;date=22/08/2026">for discussions</a> largely focused on the political and military situation in southern Lebanon, continuing Israeli attacks and <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en">the future of UNIFIL</a>, the U.N. peacekeeping mission in which Italy has the second-largest contingent – and the most of any European country. Rome <a href="https://mina.news/en/article/tajani-rome-meeting-affirms-italys-commitment-to-giving-new-impetus-to-regions-eu-path">likewise hosted</a> the latest rounds of direct talks between the Israeli and Lebanese delegations.</p>

<p>The diplomacy is part of a yearslong Italian involvement in Lebanon. Beyond its <a href="https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/08/lebanon-italy-proposes-robust-multinational-force-replace-unifil-what-know">support for UNIFIL</a>, Italy also trains Lebanese security forces and has maintained a significant diplomatic presence in the country. As UNIFIL’s mandate approaches its <a href="https://en.libnanews.com/unifil-macron-and-meloni-prepare-next/">scheduled end on Dec. 31, 2026</a>, Italy is also working with France and other partners on what might replace it and how to avoid a security vacuum. </p>

<p>In Lebanon, Italy has an established presence on the ground dating back years, a relationship with Israel, <a href="https://www.iai.it/en/publications/c05/meloni-between-trump-and-europe-limits-political-adaptability">and the ability to speak to Washington and European allies</a>. </p>

<p>Aoun’s government has a reason to want Italy involved, but that role also creates a dilemma for Meloni.</p>

<p>On Sept. 6, 2026, Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed several people, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5yl96vz0edo">according to Lebanese authorities</a>, prompting Aoun to condemn what he called a dangerous escalation and appeal for international intervention. Israel said it was responding to <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/idf-says-strikes-targeted-hezbollah-infrastructure-in-response-to-attack-on-troops/">Hezbollah attacks and was targeting</a> the militant group’s infrastructure. </p>

<p>Lebanese leaders won’t see Italy as a credible interlocutor if it ignores Israeli violations of a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-lebanon-say-they-agree-ceasefire-2026-06-03/">June 2026 ceasefire</a>. At the same time, Meloni cannot simply abandon Israel without damaging a relationship that she has spent years cultivating. </p>

<p>Yet for Meloni, Italy’s ability to maintain relationships with opposing sides provides diplomatic value, even if the process ultimately does not lead anywhere. Her approach is therefore best understood as one of political calibration: acknowledging concerns over Lebanese and Palestinian suffering, while preserving Italy’s relationship with Israel and maintaining diplomatic access to competing sides. </p>

<h2>The business of stability</h2>

<p>There is another reason Italy is becoming more active in the region: economics.</p>

<p>The Mediterranean is not simply Italy’s geographical neighborhood. It is a strategic economic space involving energy, trade, infrastructure, investment, migration and security. </p>

<p>Italy’s ties <a href="https://ambriad.esteri.it/en/italia-e-arabia-saudita/rapporti-politici/?utm">with the Gulf are not new</a>, but Meloni’s government has stepped them up, giving economic and strategic interests a more prominent role. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/interviste/2022/06/lauding-social-reforms-in-saudi-arabia-italian-foreign-minister-luigi-di-maio-says-rome-ready-to-support-kingdom/">previous government</a> was <a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/comunicati/2021/08/nota-farnesina-colloquio-telefonico-tra-il-ministro-di-maio-e-il-suo-omologo-saudita-faisal-bin-farhan-al-saud-2/">already seeking closer ties</a> with Saudi Arabia. Under Meloni, the relationship has gone further. In January 2025, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/italy-saudi-arabia-ink-10-billion-cooperation-industrial-deals-2025-01-26/">Italy and Saudi Arabia upgraded their ties</a> to a strategic partnership and signed agreements worth around US$10 billion.</p>

            <img alt="Government officials gather at a forum." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759744/original/file-20260914-50-2y5rrv.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="caption">Italy’s foreign minister, middle, hosts his Saudi and Palestinian counterparts in Rome on July 29, 2026.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>By 2026, Foreign Minister Tajani was describing the Saudi relationship as “<a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/approfondimenti/2026/08/vicepresidente-del-consiglio-dei-ministri-italiano-larabia-saudita-e-un-partner-essenziale-per-la-stabilita-regionale/">one of the pillars” of Italy’s regional engagement</a>. He has explicitly linked it to political, economic and security interests, including the protection of maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.</p>

<p>The scale of this economic relationship <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/italy-saudi-arabia-ink-10-billion-cooperation-industrial-deals-2025-01-26/">is also becoming clearer</a>. Italian <a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/comunicati/2025/06/il-ministro-tajani-presenta-il-piano-dazione-per-lexport-italiano-nei-mercati-extra-ue-ad-alto-potenziale/">exports to Saudi Arabia</a> reached around $7.2 billion in 2024, up 28% from the previous year, with Italian companies looking to take part in Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 projects in areas such as infrastructure, transport, technology, energy and tourism. </p>

<p>The United Arab Emirates <a href="https://www.esteri.it/en/sala_stampa/archivionotizie/comunicati/2025/06/il-ministro-tajani-presenta-il-piano-dazione-per-lexport-italiano-nei-mercati-extra-ue-ad-alto-potenziale/">is another important market</a>: Italian exports reached about $9.2 billion in 2024, up 21%. And during Meloni’s February 2025 visit, the UAE announced plans to invest $40 billion in Italy and signed more than 40 agreements covering areas including investment, energy, defense, space and technology. </p>

<p>The Gulf is therefore becoming more than an energy supplier or diplomatic partner for Italy. It is an increasingly important market for Italian exports, investment and business.</p>

<h2>The balancing act of diplomacy</h2>

<p>This economic dimension helps explain why Italy’s regional activism under Meloni is best understood not as a wholesale departure from previous governments but as a pragmatic <a href="https://ambriad.esteri.it/en/italia-e-arabia-saudita/rapporti-politici/">intensification of a long-standing strategy of diversification</a>, commercial diplomacy and strategic flexibility. </p>

<p>For Rome, stability in places such as Lebanon matters not only because of humanitarian and security concerns. Even though Italy’s direct <a href="https://ambbeirut.esteri.it/en/news/dall_ambasciata/2024/03/president-meloni-visits-lebanon-27-march-2024/">economic exposure</a> to Lebanon is comparatively limited, the Meloni government views Lebanese stability within a wider regional framework in which conflict can affect maritime security, energy markets, trade and investment. </p>

<p>Meloni has sought to convert Italy’s geographical position and existing relationships into economic and diplomatic leverage, while preserving room to engage with a wide range of regional actors. </p>

<p>This is consistent with a broader pattern in Italian foreign policy under Meloni: <a href="https://revdem.ceu.edu/2025/06/18/figaro-qui-figaro-qua/">less a commitment to fixed ideological positions</a> than a persistent effort to preserve room for maneuver. The Middle East now offers a particularly revealing test of that strategy.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291016/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours – and their grades quickly improved</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759229/original/file-20260910-50-asn17l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C536%2C4820%2C3213&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Half of surveyed college students said they go to bed after 1 a.m., on average. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/college-student-dormitory-vector-royalty-free-illustration/1171871744?phrase=sleep%20college%20students&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Paying college students about US$5 a night to sleep seven hours got them a quarter more nights of adequate sleep – and better grades. </p>

<p>That is what we found in a study we published <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/740221">in July 2026</a>.</p>

<p>We gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit – <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/technology/fitbit/">a wearable activity tracker</a> that looks similar to a watch – and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. We randomly chose 468 students and paid them about $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours, over the course of four weeks. We verified how much they slept using the device they wore.</p>

<p>The students were about 19 years old, on average, and half of them were first-year students. Roughly 72% of them were women. About 55% were white, 28% Asian, 9% Black and 4% Hispanic.</p>

<p>Our study shows that offering an immediate financial reward can help students meet a seven-hour sleep goal, and that those effects can persist up to a month beyond when the students are paid.</p>

<h2>Not just a student problem</h2>

<p>About one-third of American adults <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db559.htm">sleep less than seven hours</a> a night, and a similar share say they wish they slept more. Among adolescents and young adults, roughly two-thirds <a href="https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2014-1696">routinely fall short</a> of getting seven hours of sleep a night – the amount of shut-eye that <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/sleep/about/index.html">health authorities recommend</a>. </p>

<p>One prominent sleep researcher <a href="https://doi.org/10.60508/m3sw-rz13">has called sleep deprivation</a> the most prevalent high-risk behavior.</p>

<p>Short sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/65/wr/mm6506a1.htm">stroke and early death</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0543-4">Irregular sleep predicts</a> mortality risk <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2011.01.009">even more than sleep duration does</a>. Sleep loss shows up in decision-making, even when it comes to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2025.102114">issues like whether people vote</a>. </p>

<h2>Students are running on empty</h2>

<p>Before we changed anything, the average student in our study <a href="https://doi.org/10.1086/740221">slept 6.6 hours a night</a>. </p>

<p>Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average – a quarter after 2 a.m.</p>

<p>Students got the recommended seven hours of sleep on a typical weeknight on only 43% of their nights, and more than 85% fell short at least once a week.</p>

<p>They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours – the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five. </p>

<p>And 94% said their ideal night of sleep was longer than the one they were getting.</p>

<h2>What the money bought</h2>

<p>The 468 students we offered nightly payments reached seven hours of sleep on 26% more nights than 380 students who were not offered the money. That is a large shift for a group in which fewer than half were hitting the mark to begin with.</p>

<p>Students receiving the monetary incentive slept 19 more minutes per school night, roughly the difference between closing the laptop at 11:40 p.m. or at midnight. </p>

<p>Among students receiving the payment incentive, their GPA rose by about 0.08 points that semester – roughly a quarter of the gap between students who arrived with above-average and below-average high school grades. </p>

<p>Once the payments stopped after four weeks, students who had received the money were still sleeping about eight minutes longer per night for the remaining three to four weeks of the study. The effect was smaller than during our study, but our findings suggest that some of the change in sleep habits persisted for up to a month after the end of the incentive.</p>

<p>The effects of the intervention on sleep and GPA were largest among first-term freshmen, whose routines are not yet necessarily fixed. </p>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Rewards work – if they come right away</h2>

<p>Timing mattered too: Delivering the payment as a lump sum at the end of the semester, rather than every morning, produced only about two-thirds of the effect on sleep. </p>

<p>The effects of the intervention on GPA faded over a couple of academic terms. Grades remained higher in the following semester, but two semesters later we could no longer detect an effect.</p>

<p>Bedtime reminders and morning feedback on their own – with no money attached – had little effect. Students who received them slept only marginally more. The problem was not motivation: Nearly all said they wanted more sleep than they were getting. The challenge was following through on that intention night after night. </p>

<h2>Investing in sleep</h2>

<p>Our results show that universities should look at how the environment they create fosters or discourages good sleep habits. </p>

<p>Late evening deadlines to submit assignments and early classes can both make it harder for students to get enough sleep. Changing some of these features costs little compared with many academic support programs, and it may be worth testing alongside other interventions aimed directly at students.</p>

<p>Reminders and feedback might also work better if they change over time, rather than becoming familiar and easy to tune out.</p>

<p>Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder. Our results suggest they should.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289935/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>How libraries in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and other Pennsylvania communities evolved from subscription clubs to vital public institutions</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759210/original/file-20260910-50-jrcx8x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C34%2C5242%2C3494&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Pennsylvania played a vital role in the growth and spread of public libraries in America.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fleetwood-pa-a-woman-looks-through-books-in-the-fleetwood-news-photo/1367879889">Ben Hasty/MediaNews Group/Reading Eagle via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As a librarian who <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=_-5JXakAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">researches</a> and <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/">writes about library history in Pennsylvania</a>, I was delighted to see the American Library Association’s efforts to celebrate its <a href="https://ala150.org/">150th anniversary</a> this year, while making several mentions of Pennsylvania.</p>

<p>The ALA highlighted its <a href="https://ala150.org/present-at-the-creation/">1876 founding in Philadelphia</a>; how Pittsburgh philanthropist <a href="https://ala150.org/youve-got-mail-carnegie-libraries-as-seen-through-library-postcards/">Andrew Carnegie</a> funded the construction of more than 1,600 library buildings throughout the United States; and Scranton’s <a href="https://ala150.org/henry-and-edith-carr-alas-golden-couple/">Henry and Edith Carr</a>, who attended and maintained records about the ALA’s early conferences for nearly 50 years. </p>

<p>But these stories just scratch the surface of how Pennsylvanians have contributed to American libraries and librarianship.</p>

<p>I published a book on <a href="https://upittpress.org/books/9780822947004/">Pennsylvania libraries from the 1700s through the 1940s</a>, and I’m working on a sequel that extends the story to the early 2000s. Many scholars connect the beginning of public librarianship in the United States to ALA’s 1876 founding, but libraries’ roots <a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/american-libraries-before-1876-9780313312779/">go back much further</a>. </p>

<h2>America’s first ‘public’ library</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://librarycompany.org/about-lcp/">Library Company of Philadelphia</a>, established in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin, was the nation’s first successful circulating library and was a model for many others. </p>

<p>These early “public” libraries – so called because they did not require users to affiliate with churches, colleges or other organizations – were run by stockholders who pooled funds to purchase books. The owners charged annual membership fees to others who wanted to join. </p>

<p>In the 19th century there was widespread desire among U.S. educators, women’s clubs, local government leaders and public-spirited citizens to provide libraries to everyone, whether or not they could afford to subscribe. </p>

<p>Today, some people incorrectly believe that steel magnate Carnegie was the first philanthropist to donate money for library buildings. However, a number of other Pennsylvanians preceded him. </p>

<p>In 1883, for example, <a href="https://archives.house.state.pa.us/people/member-biography?ID=8250">Thomas Struthers</a>, a lawyer and land developer, constructed a <a href="https://www.strutherslibrarytheatre.org/history">multipurpose building</a> in Warren, Penn., that contained a theater and storefronts. Those spaces were to support a public library that was also in the building. The business plan didn’t work, however, and users had to purchase “tickets” to borrow books. </p>

<p>Given such situations, <a href="https://carnegie.org/about/andrew-carnegie-story/">Carnegie’s philanthropy</a> was especially impactful because it shifted some financial responsibility to local governments.</p>

<p>While some of the lavish libraries Carnegie first erected in the Pittsburgh area came with endowments – the <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/27778546">Homestead library</a> is one that still exists – he later developed a formula to ensure that other communities would not rely on his continuous generosity. As a condition of most of his grants, Carnegie insisted that municipalities provide land plus annual operating funds equivalent to at least 10% of the buildings’ costs. This effectively committed municipalities to finance libraries with public dollars. </p>

<h2>Federal and state support for public libraries</h2>

<p>In Pennsylvania, rural residents received a library boost with the passage of <a href="https://palrb.gov/getfile.cfm?file=resources/preservation-project/pltiftopdf/19001999/1931/0/act/0329.pdf&amp;view=true">Act 329</a> in 1931. The legislation offered partial matching funds to counties that provided library services.</p>

<p>Notably, the law excluded the state’s two largest counties – Philadelphia and Allegheny. </p>

<p>The federal Library Services Act of 1956-1962, a forerunner of the current <a href="https://www.imls.gov/find-funding/funding-opportunities/grants-to-states-overview">Grants to States</a> program, further aided libraries in communities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants. The funds supported book purchases and projects such as bookmobile services.</p>

<p>Until the 1960s, though, there were no parallel funding streams for larger communities. This may have compounded other inequities. </p>

<p>Pennsylvania libraries did not practice de jure racial discrimination <a href="https://www.umasspress.com/9781625341785/not-free-not-for-all/">as Southern libraries did</a>. Nor did they deliberately exclude senior citizens or people with disabilities. But how they allocated resources, designed spaces, developed collections, recruited staff and engaged local residents through specialized programming favored some constituents over others. </p>

<p>Just a few weeks ago I uncovered a <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/2026/08/knowing-better-and-doing-better.html">November 1969 article</a> in the Pennsylvania Library Association bulletin that was written by <a href="https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/honorable-augusta-clark">Augusta A. “Gussie” Clark</a>, once a librarian and later a member of Philadelphia’s City Council. Clark wrote about how she believed white librarians in the City of Brotherly Love were failing Black children. She described the librarians’ lack of respect for Black communities, their “pained tolerance” of Black people in their midst, and an unwillingness to render extra help – all of which, she said, prevented Black children from feeling “at home” in public libraries.</p>

<p>Using libraries’ records, I have also found many requests from both individuals and advocacy groups asking for ramps, elevators and other alterations to century-old libraries, and for additional listening and viewing equipment. In at least one case, a complaint reached the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights; it was investigated and ultimately dismissed.  </p>

<h2>Libraries strive to be more inclusive</h2>

<p>Libraries in urban areas of Pennsylvania began to receive state support after the  passage of Act 188 of 1961, which created a <a href="https://pa-gov.libguides.com/stateaidresources">state aid</a> program for municipal as well as county libraries. It also provided additional funding to the <a href="https://www.freelibrary.org/">Free Library of Philadelphia</a> and Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, which became Statewide Library Resource Centers. As such, they received extra funding to provide services to other libraries and customers in the state. </p>

<p>On the national level, the <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/25697349">Library Services and Construction Act</a>, which replaced the Library Services Act in 1964, did not exclude urban and populous suburban areas as the Library Services Act had. In administering the new funds, the State Library of Pennsylvania approved many proposals that extended services to underserved residents, such as Montgomery County-Norristown Public Library’s <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/2026/04/a-pastor-brings-books-to-bars-prisons.html">outreach to public housing complexes and prisons</a>, Altoona Area Public Library’s <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/2026/06/learning-is-for-everyone-altoonas.html">L.I.F.E. program</a> for people with intellectual disabilities, and Cumberland County Library System’s <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/2026/05/a-40-year-commitment-to-seniors.html">STAR service</a> for homebound senior citizens. </p>

<p>In the following decades, libraries continued to strive to become more accessible. In the 1990s the <a href="https://www.imls.gov/find-funding/funding-opportunities/grants-to-states/purpose-and-priorities-of-lsta">Library Services and Technology Act</a> and state efforts such as <a href="https://www.nga.org/governor/tom-ridge/">Gov. Tom Ridge’s</a> <a href="https://klnpa-statelibrary-pa.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/permalink/01SSHELCO_STLIBPA/9db8rh/alma9910944216803572">Link-to-Learn</a> initiative addressed the digital divide between communities that had computers and internet connections and those that did not. It provided grants for libraries to acquire needed upgrades.</p>

<p>Thirty years later, there are still some places in Pennsylvania, especially in rural and mountainous areas, that don’t have broadband. However, that number <a href="https://broadband.pa.gov/maps-data/">shrinks each year</a> thanks to <a href="https://broadband.pa.gov/shapiro-administration-plan-to-drive-out-more-than-711-million-to-connect-every-pennsylvanian-to-high-speed-internet-approved-by-ntia/">federal and state efforts</a> to build infrastructure in communities that corporate entities have neglected.</p>

<h2>Role of librarians today</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.aei.org/politics-and-public-opinion/if-libraries-are-about-finding-the-truth-lets-be-honest-about-their-decline/">Some commentators</a> argue that the internet, online databases and AI have replaced the need for public libraries and professional librarians. But a lot of information and recreational reading material is locked behind paywalls that Google and chatbots cannot circumvent.</p>

<p>Librarians today continue to play a crucial role in ensuring that resources remain available to the “largest number, at the least cost,” as American librarian <a href="https://www.libraryjournal.com/story/editorial-deweys-ala-motto-still-works-fine">Melvil Dewey articulated</a> more than a century ago. </p>

<p>The Pennsylvania Library Association has found that for every $1 in tax investment, <a href="https://www.palibraries.org/library-roi/">libraries return $5.50 in benefits</a>. This is largely by acquiring materials at discounts and enabling library customers to share and reuse them.</p>

<p>Working in today’s libraries can require substantial courage, too, given current <a href="https://pen.org/report/out-of-circulation/">censorship trends in public libraries</a>, including <a href="https://www.ala.org/bbooks/book-ban-data">book bans</a>. Requests to remove titles, or reshelve them in less-accessible areas, is nothing new. For example, I documented an example in <a href="https://palibhist.blogspot.com/2013/08/an-early-incidence-of-library.html">Scranton in 1898</a> in which Catholic citizens urged the removal of Augusta Jane Evans-Wilson’s novel “Inez: A Tale of the Alamo,” due to its negative portrayal of a priest and inaccurate descriptions of Catholic sacraments. However, current activists’ tactics are becoming more broad-stroke, aggressive and even violent.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://www.ala.org/advocacy/adverse-legislation-states">American Library Association</a> and <a href="https://www.everylibrary.org/billtracking">EveryLibrary</a>, a library advocacy group, have noted bills in various states that propose jailing library employees for the materials their institutions contain. There do not seem to be any bills presently of concern in Pennsylvania. But news reports about other book challenges and bans in Pennsylvania, <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2021/09/23/us/pennsylvania-school-book-ban-reversed">especially in school libraries</a>, regularly show up in my inbox and social media feeds. </p>

            <img alt="Woman sits in chair holding books in her hand and is surrounded by shelves of books" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=406&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759218/original/file-20260910-50-fhhtgy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=510&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Samantha Hull, a high school librarian in Lancaster, Pa., holds three books in 2022 that touch on gender identity or racism that were removed from shelves at her school. Hull has been active in the fight against book bans.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/ehprata-pa-samantha-hull-poses-for-a-portrait-with-three-news-photo/1240165367">Kyle Grantham for The Washington Post via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>When you view the centuries-long history of American librarianship through a Pennsylvania lens, it’s more complex, nuanced and fascinating than many people realize. And while today’s libraries face various challenges, I believe they continue to contribute enormously to residents across the entire state. </p>

Many scholars connect the beginning of public librarianship in the United States to ALA’s 1876 founding, but libraries’ roots go back much further

The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh has 19 branches throughout the city, including the main branch in Oakland. bgwalker/iStock/Getty Images Plus America’s first ‘public’ library The Library Company of Philadelphia , established in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin, was the nation’s first successful circulating library and was a model for many others
These early “public” libraries – so called because they did not require users to affiliate with churches, colleges or other organizations – were run by stockholders who pooled funds to purchase books
The owners charged annual membership fees to others who wanted to join

In the 19th century there was widespread desire among U.S. educators, women’s clubs, local government leaders and public-spirited citizens to provide libraries to everyone, whether or not they could afford to subscribe
Today, some people incorrectly believe that steel magnate Carnegie was the first philanthropist to donate money for library buildings
However, a number of other Pennsylvanians preceded him
In 1883, for example, Thomas Struthers , a lawyer and land developer, constructed a multipurpose building in Warren, Penn., that contained a theater and storefronts
Those spaces were to support a public library that was also in the building
The business plan didn’t work, however, and users had to purchase “tickets” to borrow books
Given such situations, Carnegie’s philanthropy was especially impactful because it shifted some financial responsibility to local governments

While some of the lavish libraries Carnegie first erected in the Pittsburgh area came with endowments – the Homestead library is one that still exists – he later developed a formula to ensure that other communities would not rely on his continuous generosity
As a condition of most of his grants, Carnegie insisted that municipalities provide land plus annual operating funds equivalent to at least 10% of the buildings’ costs
This effectively committed municipalities to finance libraries with public dollars
This library in Reading, Pa., was built with a $100,000 grant from Andrew Carnegie and opened in 1913
Ben Hasty/MediaNews Group/Reading Eagle via Getty Images Federal and state support for public libraries In Pennsylvania, rural residents received a library boost with the passage of Act 329 in 1931
The legislation offered partial matching funds to counties that provided library services
Notably, the law excluded the state’s two largest counties – Philadelphia and Allegheny
The federal Library Services Act of 1956-1962, a forerunner of the current Grants to States program, further aided libraries in communities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants
The funds supported book purchases and projects such as bookmobile services
Until the 1960s, though, there were no parallel funding streams for larger communities
This may have compounded other inequities
Pennsylvania libraries did not practice de jure racial discrimination as Southern libraries did
Nor did they deliberately exclude senior citizens or people with disabilities
But how they allocated resources, designed spaces, developed collections, recruited staff and engaged local residents through specialized programming favored some constituents over others

Just a few weeks ago I uncovered a November 1969 article in the Pennsylvania Library Association bulletin that was written by Augusta A. “Gussie” Clark , once a librarian and later a member of Philadelphia’s City Council
Clark wrote about how she believed white librarians in the City of Brotherly Love were failing Black children

She described the librarians’ lack of respect for Black communities, their “pained tolerance” of Black people in their midst, and an unwillingness to render extra help – all of which, she said, prevented Black children from feeling “at home” in public libraries

Using libraries’ records, I have also found many requests from both individuals and advocacy groups asking for ramps, elevators and other alterations to century-old libraries, and for additional listening and viewing equipment
In at least one case, a complaint reached the U.S
Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights; it was investigated and ultimately dismissed

Libraries strive to be more inclusive Libraries in urban areas of Pennsylvania began to receive state support after the passage of Act 188 of 1961, which created a state aid program for municipal as well as county libraries
It also provided additional funding to the Free Library of Philadelphia and Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, which became Statewide Library Resource Centers
As such, they received extra funding to provide services to other libraries and customers in the state
On the national level, the Library Services and Construction Act , which replaced the Library Services Act in 1964, did not exclude urban and populous suburban areas as the Library Services Act had

<title>To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree</title>
    <content type="html"><p>College students are facing one of the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/jobs/young-college-graduate-job-market-dd0f8d6e">most precarious labor markets</a> in years. A recent <a href="https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/college-labor-market#--:explore:unemployment">New York Federal Reserve study</a> pointed to a sharp increase in the post-college unemployed compared with other workers, with explanations ranging from artificial intelligence job displacement to a broader slowdown in hiring.</p>

<p>One <a href="https://www.wsj.com/us-news/education/they-chose-careers-in-the-trades-and-still-wound-up-with-debt-a68bc251">response has been a boom</a> in trade-school and apprenticeship programs that launch young people into “AI-proof” careers. But students at community and four-year colleges can also beat these headwinds and launch a career through on-the-job internships.</p>

<p><a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=7KlYIlgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">We’re a group</a> of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=pEZkS_8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">multidisciplinary scholars</a> at The Ohio State University <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=w3het8kAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">who study</a> two paid internship programs in science, technology, engineering and math, or STEM, with a proven record of landing jobs for students. Although the two initiatives use different models, they both illustrate four lessons that colleges and employers can use to turn internships into genuine career pathways. </p>

<p>Just as notable is that a large share of these students come from diverse and underrepresented backgrounds, with many being the first in their families to go to  college. <a href="https://www.coil-impact.org/batteri">These</a> <a href="https://www.coil-impact.org/drive-to-thrive">programs</a> can serve as a powerful equalizer for young people who may not otherwise have such career opportunities.</p>

<h2>Quality over quantity</h2>

<p>Internships remain one of higher education’s most powerful tools for preparing students for work. <a href="https://iro.uiowa.edu/esploro/outputs/book/How-college-affects-students-21st-century/9984285549002771">Decades of research</a> show that students who complete high-quality internships are more likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econedurev.2021.102141">secure job interviews</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/00400911011017690">high-earning positions</a> post-graduation. </p>

<p>At the same time, the number of <a href="https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/internships-are-more-crucial-than-everand-even-harder-to-find-cbefc84a">internship opportunities</a> is diminishing, even though that preparation matters more than ever. Artificial intelligence is <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-and-work-an-expert-assesses-how-far-this-revolution-still-has-to-run-277650">transforming entry-level work</a>, leading employers to <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-employers-still-place-a-premium-on-people-skills-not-ai-when-they-make-hiring-decisions-285583">increasingly value</a> the human skills that machines cannot easily replicate: judgment, adaptability, collaboration and the ability to solve unfamiliar problems. </p>

<p>Academic leaders are recognizing these pressures. More than one-third of university presidents and two-thirds of community college presidents told an Inside Higher Ed survey that they <a href="https://www.insidehighered.com/news/deep-dives/2026/02/17/why-higher-ed-leaning-apprenticeships">plan to add or expand apprenticeship pathways</a> over the next three years. </p>

<p>But it’s not just the number of internships that matters – internship quality counts just as much. </p>

<p>Our research at the <a href="https://www.coil-impact.org/">College Impact Laboratory</a> examined learning through experience with two multi-institutional studies. One is <a href="https://www.coil-impact.org/batteri">Bridging Academic Training Through Experiential Research and Innovation, or BATTERI</a>, led by principal investigator <a href="https://people.engineering.osu.edu/people/sayre.17">Jay Sayre</a> and project manager <a href="https://imr.osu.edu/about-us/contact">Joanna Gardner</a>. The other is <a href="https://www.coil-impact.org/drive-to-thrive">Drive to Thrive</a>.</p>

<p>Across both initiatives, students benefited when their experiences combined substantive work with mentoring and professional development, rather than being treated as inexpensive labor. This distinction suggests that merely placing students in workplaces isn’t enough. The structure and quality of those experiences help determine whether internships lead to meaningful, high-earning careers.</p>



<h2>Learning by doing</h2>

<p>Drive to Thrive <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/matthewmayhew/2025/12/03/the-auto-technician-pipeline-is-strong-the-problem-is-the-dealership/">deploys an approach</a> called earn-as-you-learn.  Through partnerships with Ford dealerships, students alternate between classroom instruction and paid workplace experience. They work alongside experienced technicians, diagnose and repair customers’ vehicles and receive regular coaching. </p>

<p>In this sense, it’s similar to the <a href="https://theconversation.com/german-apprenticeships-are-built-on-a-cohesive-national-plan-not-ad-hoc-partnerships-23210">European model of traineeships</a> for young people.</p>

<p>This initiative reached 635 students at 18 community colleges, including 345 first-generation students and 300 students of color. Through interviews and focus groups, a majority told us the internship helped them see themselves as true professionals. And several said the internship confirmed they had chosen the right career.</p>

<p>The numbers also backed up our approach. Students in the earn-as-you-learn program were almost 50% more likely to graduate compared with students in a matched comparison group. </p>

<p>Our other program brings together clean energy manufacturing students from three different types of institutions – a major research university, a historically Black university and a community college – for a 10-week internship. The program combines workplace learning with professional development workshops, peer networking, community engagement and projects with industry partners such as Honda, Stellantis and Schaeffler.</p>

<p>This initiative took a distinctive approach by assigning multiple mentors to each student. The idea is to help students develop relationships with faculty members, technical experts, employers and classmates. This network, in turn, strengthened students’ confidence, professional identity and sense of belonging while complementing the technical skills they develop. </p>

<p>To date, the formula has worked. More than half the participants in 2025 have already lined up either a new internship or job interviews. Industry partners also plan to rehire several members of the 2026 cohort as interns, extending their training beyond our program and opening pathways into clean-tech careers.</p>

<p>Based on this record, we believe that colleges should build broader support networks around internships rather than expect a single supervisor to shoulder the entire responsibility for a student’s professional development.</p>

<h2>Making work matter</h2>

<p>In both programs, four valuable principles emerged.</p>

<p>First is the importance of meaningful work. We believe interns should tackle real organizational challenges with deliverables that matter beyond the classroom. For example, two interns spent the summer addressing a safety challenge for Honda – how to prevent battery cells from catching fire and cooling them down when they do. </p>

<p>After developing potential solutions, they presented their work to industry representatives. A senior engineer from the Honda Research Institute was so impressed that he contacted them about a post-internship opportunity.</p>

<p>That sense of consequence changed how the students approached the work. Rather than viewing it as an assignment to complete, they were making a contribution that others depended on. </p>

<p>Second is the constellation of support for students. The liaison between the institution and industry partners is essential, serving as the connective tissue that holds the internship together and ensuring that students don’t fall through the cracks. </p>

<p>But that liaison alone isn’t enough. Students also need access to faculty, industry supervisors, technical experts and peers, since each brings a different kind of guidance. One strength of the clean energy program, for example, is its inclusion of industry experts across institutions and organizations. Students benefit most when they can draw on multiple mentors and peer support to develop key collaborative skills.</p>

<p>Third, students should learn how to normalize struggle. Internships aren’t a test of whether students can already function as professionals. They’re environments for students to try, fail and retry. When educators emphasize struggle as part of the learning process, students are encouraged to avoid perfectionism and instead ask for help when difficulties arise. </p>

<p>For example, students submit weekly reports during the clean energy program that give them the chance to discuss challenges, troubleshoot problems together and recognize that uncertainty is part of becoming a professional.</p>

<p>Finally, it’s vital to make interns’ contributions visible. Presentations, project showcases and recognition from industry professionals reinforce that students’ work matters while strengthening their professional identities. </p>

<p>We believe universities and industries alike should heed these lessons, which extend well beyond clean energy manufacturing and automotive technology. Successful programs build ecosystems that often determine whether students simply complete an internship or launch a career.</p>

<p>As colleges respond to changing labor markets, they should resist measuring success just by how many internships they create. Instead, they should ask whether those opportunities help students become confident, capable professionals. Internship quantity opens the door to better outcomes after college. Internship quality changes lives.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/288647/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

The recent history of mail voting in the United States has more twists and turns than an Emmy-winning drama
But for the cause of democracy , at least, yesterday’s ending is a happy one

On Monday, the Supreme Court definitively blocked President Donald Trump’s many attempts to sabotage voting by mail — opining, in a three-sentence brief, that Trump can’t implement his new rules for the 2026 midterms

Or for any election, probably .  Those last-minute rules, you may recall , would have required states to adopt new ballot envelopes and upload absentee voters’ names and envelope barcodes to a still-nonexistent online platform

Many officials argued they couldn’t possibly adopt the new measures before midterm voting starts, which would essentially cancel mail-in voting in their jurisdictions.  The Supreme Court, of course, has been broadly sympathetic to Trump’s legal antics, even when they appear to clearly flout law or precedent
But shutting down voting just before the midterms? That’s one bridge too far for them
Go a little deeper Hobbling vote-by-mail was just one of Trump’s plots to meddle in the midterms, however — and several of the others are still underway

Here’s where some of the president’s most significant election maneuvers stand today:  View Link How worried should you be going into the midterms? That, my friend, is a question to answer in your own little heart

But I’m taking my cues from Vox’s politics editor, Benjy Sarlin, who recently reminded listeners of our America, Actually podcast that there are many, many institutional and logistical barriers to many of Trump’s more concerning legal machinations.  “We’re taking it very seriously here…and nothing’s guaranteed,” he acknowledged. “But it is still a very difficult path [where] so far he has had zero success.” One link for later ➨ Skip the shrimp

They concluded that eating smaller animals = causing greater suffering , simply because you have to eat — and, by extension, farm and kill — so many more of them

title: Three beluga whales just died at one of America’s top-rated aquariums
excerpt: A baby beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium. | Terrence Antonio James/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images Two years ago, Marineland of Canada —
body: A baby beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium. | Terrence Antonio James/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images Two years ago, Marineland of Canada — a theme park in Niagara Falls that trained beluga whales, dolphins, and other animals to perform acrobatic tricks for entertainment — closed its doors
The decision came after years of financial turmoil, along with journalistic investigations , whistleblower accounts , and government inspections that revealed animal neglect and suffering at the park
Since 2019, 19 beluga whales and one killer whale have died at Marineland
The closure was a win for animal welfare, but where would its animals go? Marineland’s surviving menagerie included, among other species, four dolphins and 30 beluga whales

Given that beluga whales and dolphins are highly social animals that live in pods and swim long distances in the wild, animal welfare groups didn’t want to see them transferred to other parks like Marineland, or conventional aquariums, where the exceptionally smart and active animals would continue to suffer in captivity
Instead, they called for some of the 30 belugas to be rehomed to a proposed — though not yet built — 110-acre coastal sanctuary in Nova Scotia, Canada

Instead, this summer, the four dolphins and two of the beluga whales went to an aquarium in Spain, while the other belugas were transferred to two SeaWorld locations — theme parks that are similar to Marineland — and two famous US aquariums: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, which received two, and Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, which received 10
And just as Shedd’s belugas should’ve been adjusting to their new environment, things took a turn for the worse

Over the course of eight days from late August to early September, Peekachu and Rain — two belugas who arrived at Shedd Aquarium in mid-August — and another beluga whale named Beethoven, who had been at Shedd for decades, died

The three animals’ cause of death at Shedd Aquarium remains unknown as the aquarium awaits necropsy results.  While the three deaths in quick succession have put a spotlight on Shedd, they have also renewed scrutiny of a deeper problem with aquariums: their intensive confinement of wild animals, which runs throughout their history and goes beyond any one institution or animal
The limitations of aquarium life Shedd Aquarium is one of the US’s oldest and most prestigious aquariums, though this isn’t its first beluga whale controversy
Its first two belugas were taken from the wild — an estuary in Canada — in 1991

The next year, they got four more from the wild and soon after, two of them died from cardiovascular collapse after receiving an anti-parasitic drug.  “These whales died to serve a tourist attraction,” a spokesperson for the International Wildlife Coalition said at the time. “It’s horrific.” Since then, Shedd hasn’t directly sourced any beluga whales from the wild, though it’s recorded 15 beluga births in captivity
But whether taken from the wild or born in captivity, some scientists and animal advocates argue the inherent limitations of aquarium life are inhumane

One of the most outspoken among them is neuroscientist Lori Marino , an expert in marine mammal behavior and intelligence and president of the Whale Sanctuary Project, which is building the proposed Nova Scotia sanctuary
In the wild, beluga whales have far-ranging seasonal migrations, live in complex social groups, hunt for food, and raise juveniles

But Marino says that captive belugas — whether at a park like Marineland or a storied aquarium like Shedd — are in small, artificial, and unchanging environments that deny them the ability to engage in many of their natural behaviors. “The level of boredom that they experience is really unbelievable,” Marino told Vox. “For an animal like that, with a brain like that, that’s torture.” A Shedd spokesperson told me that research it participated in — along with other zoological institutions — found that ensuring that animal enclosures are dynamic, well managed, contain enrichment activities, and facilitate strong socialization do more to predict good welfare than the volume of space they’re allotted
However, such artificial environments can lead to serious welfare problems
It’s not uncommon for marine mammals — and other animals in zoos and aquariums — to display “stereotypic” behavior, or repetitive motions that are indicators of stress
They might endlessly swim in circles or other patterns , continually regurgitate and reingest food , repetitively move their heads , or grate their teeth on hard surfaces
Critics call it “ zoochosis .” Some researchers believe captivity may induce depressive-like states in some animals
Zoos and aquariums tend to downplay the harms of captivity and, instead, position themselves as stewards of the animals at their facilities and protectors of their counterparts in the wild
Some animal advocates , including Marino, often argue this is largely a facade to justify the continued captivity of the animals
Are aquariums for animals, or us? Known as “the Fish House,” the first modern aquarium opened in 1853 at the London Zoo

At the time, zoos and aquariums were pitched to the public as pure entertainment — places for city dwellers to see exotic animals from far away lands up close.  But as the modern environmental and animal welfare movements matured in the middle of the 20th century, they began to question the practice of putting wild-caught animals on display in enclosures that amounted to a minuscule fraction of their range in nature
By the 1970s, in response to the criticisms, some aquariums and zoos began to pivot from marketing themselves as entertainment venues to being invested in the conservation of wildlife

Zoos and aquariums posit that if we’re to protect wild animals in, well, the wild , it makes sense that helping the public gain an affinity for them in a not-so-wild setting is an important part of the equation

Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium, for example, describes  its mission as “sparking compassion, curiosity and conservation for the aquatic animal world.”  Aquariums and zoos often say they achieve these goals by raising a lot of money for conservation projects, helping to reintroduce vulnerable species back into the wild, and inspiring visitors to get involved in conservation
In 2022, the 238 zoos and aquariums accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) — of which Shedd is a member — spent $252 million on projects to protect and preserve wildlife habitats

It’s a lot of money, though it amounts to about 5 percent of what AZA members had spent on operations and construction.  The evidence is even thinner on aquariums’ and zoos’ claims around helping to reintroduce endangered species back into the wild, as it’s an incredibly difficult and rare feat , and on motivating attendees to become conservation advocates
Some surveys of zoo-goers have found that zoo attendance can modestly improve their conservation knowledge and behavior
But despite some 700 million annual visits , far fewer visitors volunteer or donate to protect animals in the wild
Despite the heavy conservation messaging, animal advocates argue that entertainment is still the priority for most zoological institutions
According to the AZA , 80 percent of the animals in its member aquariums are taken from the wild, which seems to be in direct conflict with protecting animals in the wild

Shedd Aquarium declined an interview request for this story, and when I asked a spokesperson what percent of its 32,000 animals were taken from the wild, they wouldn’t say.  “Acquiring animals from the wild is not contrary to conservation goals as long as species are acquired in an ethical and sustainable manner,” an AZA spokesperson said over email. “These are thought-out and strategic actions with sustainability in mind.” However, AZA didn’t define how to ethically and sustainably take animals from the wild.  And Shedd — like many other aquariums — encourages guests to pay for “encounter” experiences with beluga whales and other wild, non-domesticated species, like penguins, sea lions, and otters, at up to $205 a pop

These often involve the guests having a few minutes to pet the animals and take photographs with them. (The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has temporarily prohibited Shedd and other facilities from using the rehomed belugas in encounter programs.) A Shedd spokesperson told me the criticism of these encounter programs as inhumane and unethical is “unfounded and indeed contradictory,” citing a study about dolphins that it participated in
The study, however, wasn’t designed to measure how encounter programs affect dolphin welfare, but rather looked at how dolphins use their habitat, with encounter programs as one variable among many

A 2021 literature review on encounter programs found that most research on them lacked rigor and that “the justification for using [encounter programs] within zoos remains questionable.” As for the belugas at Shedd, Marino told me she hopes that they survive, but says this moment should lead to more honest conversations about the ethics of aquariums

Institutions like Shedd “are supposed to be the best,” Marino said. “But people need to understand that it’s the best of something that doesn’t work. … It’s not a question of who’s accredited, who’s not
It’s about keeping these animals in tanks for entertainment
